section.title: Carey Nachenberg: From Symantec Fellow to Google X, Project Taste, and Imposter Syndrome
section.deck: Nachenberg says that choosing impactful projects, focusing on other people's outcomes, communicating well and leaving jobs once learning stops mattered more to his career than raw intelligence, and that imposter syndrome held him back.

blocks.text: Nachenberg, a former Symantec fellow who later worked at Google X, Chronicle and Lyft and now teaches at UCLA, argues that career growth owes far more to project taste, focus on other people's outcomes, and communication than to raw intelligence. He traces his own rise at Symantec to choosing impactful projects nobody had assigned. He says imposter syndrome and a loss of confidence kept him in a comfortable job too long and later held him back at Google. The conversation ends with his views on how large language models (LLMs) change teaching, software engineering and product work, and with the advice he would give his younger self.
blocks.heading: Impact, outcomes and communication outweigh raw intelligence

blocks.question: Can you give the high-level story of your time at Symantec and how you grew to fellow?
answer: Nachenberg started in about 1992 as an intern at the Peter Norton Group, which Symantec later acquired. He thinks he was the first intern there and says the company had no desk for him, so he worked in the QA lab. By the time he left in 2016, he had gone from the most junior person to the most senior engineer at Symantec.

followups.question: Did you set out to work in cyber security, or did it happen by chance?
answer: By chance. Nachenberg first worked on a file-management utility, not security. In his third internship, Symantec bought an antivirus product and renamed it Norton Antivirus. The team that analyzed computer viruses needed an intern, and he was placed there with no experience.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: What did the career ladder look like at Symantec, and how did hiring work for someone as senior as you when you joined Google?
answer: Nachenberg says the levels tracked those at Google and Meta from junior engineer up to staff. They differed at the top, with distinguished engineer and fellow at Symantec. Google told him it could not hire a fellow without knowing how he would perform there. He was effectively downgraded to principal engineer, level 8, from what he says would have been about a level 10 and a vice president role at Symantec.

followups.question: Was your hiring process tailored to your seniority?
answer: Yes. Nachenberg did not apply. A former Symantec chief operating officer had moved into Google X, where a stealth project was starting, and invited him to talk to the team. He had a meet and greet with the founders in Venice, then about eight interviews in a day. He had an offer letter roughly six weeks later.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

followups.question: Did that loop include LeetCode-style coding, or was it mostly behavioral?
answer: Nachenberg does not recall any coding problems and thinks there was one design problem. Most questions were leadership-style: how he solved a hard problem, how he handles conflict, and where the field is going. Some sessions were effectively sales pitches about where Google X thought the world was heading. He believes the team already thought he was a good fit, so the day was mostly about going through the motions and selling him on the role.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: What do promotions at the highest levels look like?
answer: At Symantec, Nachenberg says, promotions up to senior technical director were handled within the organization, provided a vice president or senior vice president agreed. Distinguished engineer and fellow went to a core group of technologists led by the chief technology officer. The group met quarterly, reviewed applications, and had candidates present their work. The aim was a consistent bar across the whole company, not division by division.

followups.question: Was your promotion to fellow a big moment, or something you expected?
answer: Nachenberg skipped that process. After Symantec merged with Veritas, which already had a fellow role, the company needed to set the level. He was nominated without his knowledge, his portfolio was passed to the evaluators, and he was told he was a fellow.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: What set you apart from other engineers on the way to fellow?
answer: Nachenberg credits impactful projects, not always the most technically difficult ones. He looked for gaps: things the company needed that no one was stepping up to do. Symantec in his early years was, in his words, the wild west, with no agile process and no engineers testing their own code. He was never handed a boxed-in project. Because he already knew the technology as an intern, he was told to work out what to do and do it, and he says he chose projects that landed, shipped and transferred into the product.

followups.question: How did you train your project taste?
answer: Nachenberg says he looks for large business impact and for gaps. His example was polymorphic viruses, which mutated themselves into huge numbers of variants. Teams hand-wrote assembly to catch each variant, a process that took six months because the product shipped twice a year. New variants appeared the next day. He saw a need to respond faster, noted that such threats could not be found by searching for a string, and picked the problem. It became his master's thesis and then a product feature.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

followups.question: Was your career a series of self-chosen side projects?
answer: Partly. Nachenberg says that perhaps six or seven times he spotted a company need and spent from six weeks to five months on prototypes and talking to engineers. About 80 percent of his career was then incremental work on those systems, such as helping transfer the technology into products, fixing bugs and improving them.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: Can you tell the story of Stuxnet, which you used in talks?
answer: Nachenberg calls Stuxnet unfathomable for its time: probably the first multiplatform malware discovered, reaching Windows machines and the controllers that ran centrifuge frequency converters. He recalls it used about six vulnerabilities, many of them unpatched zero-days. It hid itself on a USB drive, auto-launched, and hid its own logic on the controller. If someone downloaded the controller logic, it removed itself from the copy. If they uploaded updated logic, it reinserted itself.

followups.question: Who do you think wrote it, and did you analyze the code?
answer: Nachenberg says it is fairly safe to say the Israeli and American governments, and he recalls coding styles that implicate both. He stresses he did not analyze Stuxnet himself. Early in his career he disassembled malware by hand, but later he built algorithms to detect it.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

followups.question: Did you write assembly at Symantec?
answer: As an intern, yes, though most code was in C. The first antivirus engines were in assembly for speed. Nachenberg ported one to C after joining full time. It had less code and ran about five times faster, he says, because the original developers did not know algorithms. In his example, hash tables or binary search replace a linear scan over about 60,000 signatures, with no help from an optimizing compiler.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: What kept you at Symantec for so long?
answer: Nachenberg says, honestly, imposter syndrome. At Symantec he felt secure because he was well known there. He worried that his success came from having grown up in that company, and that he might not be good enough for Google or Meta. He stayed because it was comfortable and he complained a lot. Near the end he was unhappy, since senior roles bring more meetings and less building, which he describes as a lot of BS.

followups.question: What helped you overcome it?
answer: An outside pull. Someone at Google X said they wanted to interview him. Nachenberg was sure he would fail but went ahead. He says he needed that push to take the chance, and it worked out.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

followups.question: How do you avoid the BS at senior levels?
answer: Nachenberg says some senior people stay hands-on, but as an individual-contributor vice president he found the strategy meetings inevitable. They bring many opinions, debate and power posturing. His best moments were picking his own projects and going two months with no one asking what he was doing. He gives one example: he wrote Symantec's technology strategy and the CEO agreed with it, but product teams then objected because of revenue targets. He calls those debates draining.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: What was Google X like, and were there cultural differences?
answer: Fewer than expected, Nachenberg says. The main difference was the quality of the people, who were very smart, whereas Symantec lacked an engineering culture, at least until it began to form around 2016. What was the same was that many people lacked project taste. They were smart, but he doubted they picked projects that would land or were feasible. He says this is true of engineers at any company.

followups.question: Why was one very bright colleague still at a low level?
answer: Nachenberg describes a colleague he judged astoundingly brilliant who was still at L4. He says the reasons were weak communication, work that interested the colleague but had little business impact, and apparently poor collaboration. He concludes that intelligence alone does not guarantee success.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

followups.question: If intelligence matters less, what matters more?
answer: Nachenberg says a baseline is needed and that most Google engineers had it. He does not consider himself especially intelligent and says he learns slowly. Beyond that baseline he names communication and collaboration, including getting what you need from people without telling them they are wrong. He admits he has not mastered this and has failed at it. The big one, he says, is focusing on outcomes: engineers naturally focus on their own, such as making something 10 percent faster, but the company or another team has different outcomes. Identify those, the metrics behind them, and the few requirements that matter most, and he says that will take you much further than intelligence.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

followups.question: Is career growth in industry meritocratic?
answer: By and large, yes, in Nachenberg's experience. He saw exceptions where a senior vice president pushed a promotion mainly to retain someone, which he says damages standards. The committees he sat on weighed the complexity and impact of work, communication and patents. He also found Google's discussions careful and fair. In his view senior levels required being well rounded, or at least very strong in some areas.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: How did Chronicle begin inside Google X, and what did its product do?
answer: Nachenberg says it started as the stealth Project Lantern, with no fixed product. The team spent about six months deciding what to build, then built prototypes and an MVP. Before the product existed, they sat in customer security teams and watched where they struggled, which he found very useful.

The product, Backstory, treated security as a big-data problem. Firewalls, web proxies, DHCP and email systems produce huge logs. Nachenberg says a competing product forced customers to ingest a small fraction of that data and wait about 30 minutes per query. Chronicle ingested petabytes and indexed them, so an analyst could enter a file hash, IP address or file name and see affected devices and first and last infiltration in about two seconds. Nachenberg worked on the indexing.

followups.question: Why did Chronicle spin out and then return to Google?
answer: Nachenberg says X aims to incubate viable businesses, give strong teams freedom and spin them out. He says he can only guess at why Chronicle came back, and that it fit Google Cloud as a storage- and compute-heavy cloud service. After the spin-out it stayed under Alphabet, like Waymo. One benefit was one-page performance reviews in a slide, instead of Google's long written packets.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: Why did you eventually leave Google?
answer: Nachenberg again cites imposter syndrome, plus a wish to work at a startup instead of a slower, more regulated environment. He says there were big problems he could have taken on, such as moving Chronicle's expensive storage design off heavyweight systems like Spanner. He lacked the confidence to try. Expectations at senior levels are high, and at Google he did not feel leadership would back him if a months-long attempt did not land. At Symantec his managers had known him for years and gave him rope. He was offered other roles, such as secure databases that compute on encrypted data. He wanted something new, and talks with Waymo people while at X had made him want to work on self-driving cars.

followups.question: Did you consider asking for a demotion to reduce the pressure?
answer: Not at Symantec, where he could do what he liked. He thought about it at Google but concluded it would not help. Even at lower levels, he says, there are expectations he might not meet if he went off for a couple of months to think, which is how he had been most successful. He calls himself a loosey-goosey prototyper who does not enjoy testing every edge case. Google expects that, so he would have had to do things he disliked to do the things he wanted.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: How did you get hired into autonomous vehicles at Lyft?
answer: A former UCLA student who worked at Lyft urged Nachenberg to apply. He doubted they would hire him. He had tried to move to Waymo from X and had not been taken, which he attributes to being senior, expensive and without domain expertise. The student arranged a meeting with Lyft's president, followed by seven or eight interviews that included some coding and design. He says there was no dynamic programming, which he says he would fail, and he was hired.
blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: What project at Lyft were you most proud of?
answer: Nachenberg says Lyft used the classic robotics architecture of hand-written decision algorithms with hand-tuned parameters, with neural networks used only for perception. He thought that was a dead end, citing conflicts such as switching from a lane-change routine to an avoidance routine, and parameters that interact in unpredictable ways. He says Tesla used the approach until recently.

He designed, with the team's old-school roboticists, an architecture that could host an end-to-end neural-network driver inside a safety layer. In his account the layer takes precedence, preventing collisions, stopping safely and following legal rules the network might miss. He guesses Waymo now uses end-to-end networks too, but says he does not know. He says the work was mostly influence, since he had no robotics degree and the roboticists resisted. They defined the approach together so that they could own it.

followups.question: How do you make sure you get credit for shared work?
answer: Nachenberg says he lacks a good recipe and was not credited for this project; he says someone else took credit. He advises juniors to take notes when a project ends, recording accomplishments and metrics, which are hard to recall later. When writing a review, state what you did and its value without embellishing, and claim only your own parts, because committees notice overclaiming and it costs credibility. At senior levels it is harder, he says, because the work is soft power. He did not push his own credit so as not to alienate collaborators, and at review time he learned the team's manager was seen as having initiated the project. He says it still bothers him.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

followups.question: What was Lyft's plan to win in self-driving?
answer: Nachenberg says it was not clear that there was a strategy. Lyft's effort was young compared with the roughly decade-long work at Google X and Waymo. He joined to learn and work with smart people, not to beat Waymo. The division was eventually sold to a Toyota subsidiary, which received the intellectual property, and he then retired.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: How did you become a lecturer at UCLA, and how do you make your lectures engaging?
answer: Nachenberg taught programming at Learning Tree around 1990 to 1991, including to DeVry staff. He also ran evening whiteboard sessions at UCLA as an undergraduate. Years later, a colleague at Symantec who lectured part time at UCLA told him to apply. Nachenberg assumed his lack of a PhD ruled him out. After months of silence, UCLA called in a panic when a lecturer dropped out, and he had two weeks to plan an undergraduate course. That was about 25 years ago.

For lectures, he designs for roughly the 30th to 50th percentile of the class, and uses himself, a slow learner, as the model. He asks what he would want to know on first meeting a topic, and what students are likely to be fuzzy on. He says he spends days with ChatGPT o3 simplifying concepts, then checks with Gemini and compares differences, because he finds good online material scarce and textbooks poor. He also wants students to enjoy class, so he adds humor, color and surprise.

followups.question: What tips do you have for public speaking?
answer: Practice, says Nachenberg. He finds his own speaking declines within a year of not using it. He suggests giving a lunchroom talk about a project even when nothing requires it. People appreciate it, and you improve. He recalls giving his Stuxnet and malware talk privately inside X, after which colleagues said he was one of the smartest people they had met. He says people read good communication as intelligence, and it brings credit and opportunities.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: Are students cheating more with LLMs, and are they learning less?
answer: Nachenberg says last fall he allowed LLMs for autocomplete and simple, peripheral parts of projects. In retrospect he considers it a mistake, because students used them for much more than that. He saw large gaps between perfect project scores and poor exam results. He mentions a recent study on reduced brain connectivity when people use LLMs, but says he forgets the numbers. This fall he plans to allow LLMs for clarifying concepts, but not for projects.

He says plagiarism software compares every project with every other one, and LLM use shows up as shared word-for-word error messages, variable names and idioms. He adds that the latest models could probably earn about 95 percent on the projects, with poor code, because the course grades correctness, not code quality.
blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: Should people still get a software engineering degree as LLMs automate the work?
answer: Nachenberg says it depends on how the models develop, and he describes two scenarios. In the first, models stay very good but short of what he calls AGI programming: they solve tightly specified sub-problems and write tests, but need supervision on choices such as the algorithm used or a deep versus shallow copy. In that world, he says, software engineering stays a great field. Someone must read the code, understand the company's mission and standards, and decide what to fix. He thinks the ability to read and write code is valuable. He acknowledges that jobs are down now, probably partly because of LLMs.
In the second scenario, an AI could take on an L5-level project that takes weeks and do it correctly and securely. He says all bets are off in that world and the required skills differ.

followups.question: What skills would matter in that second world?
answer: Nachenberg says engineers, or perhaps no longer engineers, would focus on what to build and why, not how. The best would deeply understand a customer's pains and how the customer measures success, then communicate those requirements clearly to an LLM. Clarification and outcome analysis would be the key skills. He expects big companies to remain, but thousands of smaller companies to serve niches such as pet sitters and doggy daycares, built by domain experts with these tools.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

followups.question: Is that essentially a product manager, with the LLM as the engineering team?
answer: Yes, Nachenberg says, a competent product manager, though he says he has met very few. In his view competence means understanding customer outcomes and the metrics customers use, using methods such as jobs to be done or outcome-driven innovation. His own example is that he drools when brushing his teeth, and the mess is a metric by which he would judge a toothbrush. He says many product managers think in features and copy competitors instead of finding what customers struggle with, how often, and whether it matters. He also holds that empathy can be a repeatable process built on interviews and observation. He allows that there may be exceptions.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: Looking back, is there anything you regret or would change?
answer: Nachenberg says he should have left Symantec earlier. His rule is to stay while you are learning, building skills and feel free to fail occasionally. He lost that at Symantec, but stayed because he lacked confidence, not because the work interested him. He still values staying five or even ten years as long as you learn. Switching teams can keep a good reputation and institutional knowledge. Staying too long makes you stale and comfortable.

He also notes the cost of leaving. At Symantec he was widely known and appeared on TV and in major newspapers about Stuxnet. At Google nobody cared what he had done before, so he had to rebuild trust and reputation, which is stressful.

followups.question: What about golden handcuffs, where you earn well but no longer learn?
answer: Nachenberg would never say to leave a good package. People need different amounts of money to feel safe, and people balance several things. Being comfortable and well paid for a while can be fine. But for someone who is solving for enjoyment and hard problems, he thinks too long in that state can become toxic.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: How can someone find what they enjoy in software engineering?
answer: Nachenberg advises students to try many internships, though he acknowledges jobs are tough now and the market is cyclical. He found cyber security by chance, through three different internships. He says jobs that sound boring can turn out to contain interesting problems, good colleagues and interesting customers. His advice is not to wait for the perfect job, but to find a good manager, hard problems and room to learn, which might lead to a 25-year career.

followups.question: Is the approach to search broadly first, then go deep?
answer: Yes, Nachenberg says. But if a first-year internship is interesting and going well, he would stay with it. He calls the approach a greedy breadth search.
followups.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg

blocks.question: If you could advise yourself on graduating from UCLA, what would you say?
answer: Nachenberg says there is no single item. First, do not let fear of failure hold you back. You can probably do more than you think, and he says he might have had a richer career had he listened. Second, focus on outcomes: who will use the work, what they care about and how they measure success. Problems often need a small square piece, not a perfect round thing.

He says he once presented technology to senior leaders, who did not care how the algorithm worked. They wanted to know whether it was faster, by how much, and what it meant for revenue or headcount. Speak to their needs, not your own. Third, find a good manager who trusts you and gives you rope, since a manager can make or break your career and happiness. Fourth, learn to collaborate and not assume you are right and tell others they are wrong. He says he still struggles with this.
blocks.speaker: Carey Nachenberg
